PHSCS 587

Work functions and affinity

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows which energy differences define work function and electron affinity

Before joining materials, a common vacuum reference helps organize their electron energies. Write qΦm = Evac − EFm for the metal work-function energy and qΦs = Evac − EFs for the semiconductor work-function energy. Electron affinity is qχ = Evac − EC. Here Φ and χ are expressed as volt-equivalent quantities and q times them is energy; the same numerical values are often quoted in eV for an electron.

For an ideal clean metal–n-semiconductor interface without an additional interface dipole, the Schottky–Mott electron barrier is φBn = Φm − χ. The semiconductor work function additionally depends on EF relative to EC, so doping can change Φs without changing electron affinity in the simple rigid-band model. Real interfaces can depart strongly from this ideal barrier prediction.

Build a contact diagram in stages. Separate materials can each be in equilibrium with their own chemical potential. Connecting them through a conducting wire allows charge to redistribute and establishes a common equilibrium Fermi level, while facing surfaces separated by a gap can hold capacitor-like charge. Bringing the surfaces into physical contact then introduces the interface’s bonding, states and dipole. Follow the common energy reference and the electrostatic shifts through each stage.

The same bookkeeping enters MOS flat-band voltage. In an ideal charge-free oxide, VFB = Φg − Φs using consistent voltage units. A fixed oxide sheet charge Qox′ adds a term −Qox′/Cox′ in the elementary model. Zero applied bias establishes equilibrium, but flat semiconductor bands occur at Vg = VFB and therefore can require a nonzero gate voltage.

Example

Two gates with different work functions on the same ideal semiconductor require different flat-band gate voltages even when oxide thickness is unchanged. Their oxide capacitance can be identical while their C–V curves are shifted horizontally.

Practice

1. Why does electron affinity stop at EC rather than EF?

Compare the two definitions in the figure.

Affinity references the conduction-band edge. Work function references the chemical potential and consequently also depends on EF’s location relative to that edge.

2. Does zero applied gate bias guarantee flat bands?

Consider Φg − Φs.

Flat bands require the applied voltage to match VFB. A work-function difference or oxide charge can make VFB nonzero.
